items.title: refactor(request)!: derive body representations from the cached bytes
items.body:
`HonoRequest` caches each body representation (`json`, `text`, `formData`, ...) and converts between them when the body is read again in a different way. Every conversion loses something: the media type, the multipart boundary, or a rejected promise. #5129, #5365, and #5383 were each fixed by adding a special case to the conversion, and #5294 is the next one.

This PR removes the conversion itself, so this class of bugs cannot happen again, and the special cases go away. It keeps one source of truth and derives the other representations from it:

- If the body is first read as `json()` or `text()`, the text is the source. Other representations are built from it.
- Otherwise, the bytes from `arrayBuffer()` are the source.
- `json()` caches its result, so it returns the same object every time.

Reading the same representation again returns the cache as before. Reading a different one no longer goes through a lossy conversion.

Related: #5129, #5365, #5383 (fixed individually in v4), #5294 (no longer needed with this change).

### Performance

`c.req.json()` is as fast as before. `benchmarks/fetch` (`body POST /json`) against `v5`: Bun 1.01x, Node 1.01x.

### Behavior change

When the bytes are rebuilt from the cached text, they can differ from the original (e.g., a BOM). In that case, `cloneRawRequest()` drops the `Content-Length` header and lets the runtime set it.

### The author should do the following, if applicable

- [x] Add tests
- [x] Run tests
- [x] `bun run format:fix && bun run lint:fix` to format the code
- [ ] Add [TSDoc](https://tsdoc.org/)/[JSDoc](https://jsdoc.app/about-getting-started) to document the code

items.title: formData() after text() silently corrupts binary file uploads
items.body:
### What version of Hono are you using?

4.13.13 (also reproduces on `main` at decda78a, and on the branches of #5385 and #5536)

### What runtime/platform is your app running on? (with version if possible)

Node.js v24.1.0 (reproduced with `app.request()`)

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

If a handler (or a middleware before it) reads `c.req.text()` and then calls `c.req.formData()` on a multipart request, binary file parts come back with every non-UTF-8 byte replaced by U+FFFD:

```js
import { Hono } from 'hono'

const app = new Hono()
app.post('/', async (c) => {
  await c.req.text()
  const file = (await c.req.formData()).get('file')
  return c.json([...new Uint8Array(await file.arrayBuffer())])
})

const fd = new FormData()
fd.append('file', new Blob([new Uint8Array([0xff, 0x00, 0x41])]), 'x.bin')
console.log(await (await app.request('/', { method: 'POST', body: fd })).text())
```

### What is the expected behavior?

`[255,0,65]`: the uploaded bytes unchanged. Failing loudly would also be better than silently returning different bytes.

### What do you see instead?

`[239,191,189,0,65]`: `0xff` became `EF BF BD`. The request succeeds, so the corrupted file goes through without any error.

### Additional information

`#cachedBody` rebuilds the `formData` representation from the cached `text()` result. Decoding the multipart body as UTF-8 is lossy for binary parts, and since #5366 the original multipart `Content-Type` is carried over. That makes `formData()` succeed on the lossy text. Before #5366 (e.g. 4.13.7), the same sequence threw `Content-Type was not one of "multipart/form-data" ...` and returned a 500.

#5385 keeps "text is the source when the body was first read as `text()`/`json()`". Its notes mention byte differences such as a BOM, but this case affects any binary upload, and it still reproduces on that branch. Possible directions: keep the raw bytes as the source and derive `text()` from them, or refuse to build `formData()`/`arrayBuffer()`/`blob()` from cached text when the content is multipart.

Found while backtesting an AI code-review tool on recently merged PRs. I verified the behaviour above by hand.

items.title: feat(jwt,jwk): add a configurable WWW-Authenticate realm
items.body:
Refs #4989.

`jwt` and `jwk` build their `401` challenge with the request URL hardcoded as the realm:

```ts
'WWW-Authenticate': `Bearer realm="${opts.ctx.req.url}",error="...",error_description="..."`
```

RFC 6750 describes `realm` as a stable, human-readable name for the protection space. Reflecting the full URL yields a different realm for every path and query string, which is not what the parameter is for:

```
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="https://api.example.com/v1/users/42?token=abc",...
```

`bearer-auth` already exposes a `realm` option. `jwt` and `jwk` had no equivalent, and `unauthorizedResponse()` is private in both, so there was no way to override it short of replacing the middleware.

### Changes

**A `realm` option on both middlewares**, matching `bearer-auth`:

```ts
app.use('/auth/*', jwt({ secret: 'a-secret', alg: 'HS256', realm: 'my-api' }))
// WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="my-api",error="invalid_request",error_description="..."
```

**Quote escaping.** Separately from the realm question, `realm` and `error_description` were interpolated into a quoted-string with no escaping, so a `"` in either truncates the header. Both now get the same `.replace(/"/g, '\\"')` treatment `bearer-auth` applies. This is reachable through the realm option, and `ctx.req.url` is not guaranteed to be percent-encoded on every runtime.

### On the default

The issue proposes defaulting `realm` to `""` instead of `ctx.req.url`. I have **kept the existing default** so this stays non-breaking — anyone relying on the current header sees no change, and the new behavior is opt-in.

Flipping the default is a one-line change (`opts.realm ?? ''`) and I'm happy to make it here if you'd rather correct the default outright — it just seemed like your call rather than mine, so I didn't bundle a behavior change into an additive PR.

### Verification

- `bunx vitest --run --project main` — 3657 passed, 0 failed (121 files)
- `tsc -p tsconfig.spec.json` clean, `eslint src/middleware/jwt src/middleware/jwk` 0 errors, `prettier` clean
- 7 tests added across `jwt/index.test.ts` and `jwk/index.test.ts`. The 5 realm/escaping cases fail without the source commits (verified by stashing them); the 2 default-behavior cases pass either way and exist to guard the unchanged default.

### The author should do the following, if applicable

- [x] Add tests
- [x] Run tests
- [x] `bun run format:fix && bun run lint:fix` to format the code
- [x] Add [TSDoc](https://tsdoc.org/)/[JSDoc](https://jsdoc.app/about-getting-started) to document the code

items.title: fix(etag): compute correct digest for bodies >= CHUNK_SIZE (streaming SHA-1, not hash-of-hash)
items.body:
Closes #5212.

## Root cause

PR #5205 replaced the buffer-and-hash-once logic from #5199 with a chunked accumulator to bound memory, but the chunked path recomputes the digest as `hash(hash(chunk1) + chunk2)`. Since the default generator (`crypto.subtle.digest({ name: 'SHA-1' })`) is a one-shot, stateless hash, re-hashing a digest concatenated with the next 256 KiB chunk does **not** reconstruct `SHA-1(full body)`. For any response body >= 256 KiB (CHUNK_SIZE), the emitted ETag no longer matches the real SHA-1 of the body.

#5205 fixed the *determinism* symptom of #5199 (same content -> same ETag regardless of network chunking) but silently dropped *mathematical correctness* for large bodies.

## Fix

Compute a real streaming digest instead of re-hashing digests:

- The built-in SHA-1 path now uses an **incremental** hasher when the runtime exposes one:
  - Bun: `Bun.CryptoHasher`
  - Node.js: `node:crypto.createHash`, reached via `process.getBuiltinModule` (no static `node:` import, so edge bundlers such as Cloudflare Workers can still skip it)
- Each stream chunk is fed to the hasher and discarded, so memory stays bounded.
- On runtimes without an incremental primitive (Cloudflare Workers: Web Crypto is one-shot; also Deno and older Node.js) and for user-supplied one-shot `generateDigest` functions, the middleware buffers the full body and hashes it once (the #5199 approach). This is the only correct option there and matches the documented `generateDigest` contract.

## Tests

- RED (fails before this change): a 300 KiB body must produce an ETag equal to the real SHA-1 of the full body; the same holds for a custom SHA-256 `generateDigest`.
- The existing determinism test (same 1 MiB content delivered with different stream chunk boundaries -> same ETag) still passes.
- Full etag test scope: 20 tests pass under both Bun and Node; the full hono suite (4765 tests) passes.

## Notes

- Determinism is preserved: the digest depends only on the byte sequence, not on stream chunk boundaries, on both the incremental and buffered paths.
- The >= 256 KiB case is where #5205's value was wrong; this restores correctness there without reintroducing unbounded buffering on runtimes that support streaming hashes.

items.title: feat: dispatch notFound and onError handlers as internal routes
items.body:
Taken in isolation as a solution to #5193, this may look over-engineered. The broader goal of this PR is to model error and not-found handling using Hono's own routing system. The current proposal does this through the new `catch()` and `catchNotFound()` APIs while leaving the existing `onError()` and `notFound()` semantics unchanged. Existing applications should not require any changes.

The implementation increases the minified bundle size by 3.35%. In particular, however, the single-handler fast path used by successful requests without middleware remains structurally unchanged, and local benchmarks show no performance regression.

## Summary

This draft introduces routable middleware for error and not-found handling:

```ts
app.catchNotFound(
  languageDetector(),
  (c) => c.html(render404Page(c.get('language')))
)

app.catch(
  languageDetector(),
  (c) => c.html(renderErrorPage(c.get('language'), c.error), 500)
)
```

Unlike `onError()`, `catch()` uses the normal middleware signature `(c, next)`. The caught error is available as `c.error`.

The middleware can also be scoped explicitly by path:

```ts
api.catch('/items/*', (c) =>
  c.text(`items error: ${c.error?.message}`, 500)
)

api.catchNotFound('/items/*', (c) =>
  c.text('items not found', 404)
)
```

These definitions are registered with reserved internal methods, `@ERROR` and `@NOT_FOUND`, and selected through the configured Router.

The existing final handlers remain unchanged:

```ts
app.onError((error, c) => c.text(error.message, 500))
app.notFound((c) => c.text('Not Found', 404))
```

If all matching `catch()` or `catchNotFound()` middleware calls `next()`, execution reaches the corresponding legacy handler.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The existing APIs remain compatible, but this changes internal fallback dispatch, adds reserved internal routes, and adds route-depth metadata. This is still a PoC and should be evaluated with a major version in mind.

## Why internal routes?

A definition such as:

```ts
app.catchNotFound(
  languageDetector(),
  renderNotFound
)
```

can be understood as a route definition that is internally dispatched when a not-found response is requested.

This gives fallback middleware the useful properties of normal route middleware:

- middleware composition
- path and base-path scoping
- sub-application flattening
- Router-level wrapping and instrumentation
- preservation of metadata describing where an error or explicit not-found originated

The internal dispatch reuses the existing `Context`, request path, and route metadata. It does not create another `Request` or restart the whole application middleware chain.

## New APIs

### `catch()`

`catch()` adds middleware that runs when an error is caught:

```ts
app.catch(async (c, next) => {
  console.error(c.error)
  await next()
})
```

A middleware may:

- call `next()` to continue through the matching error middleware
- modify the response after `next()`
- return a response without calling `next()` to stop the chain
- throw another error, which is passed to the legacy `onError()` handler

If every matching middleware calls `next()`, the current legacy `onError(error, c)` handler produces the final response.

### `catchNotFound()`

`catchNotFound()` adds middleware that runs when a not-found response is requested:

```ts
app.catchNotFound(async (c, next) => {
  c.header('x-not-found', 'true')
  await next()
})
```

It is used for both:

- implicit not-found handling
- a returned `c.notFound()` response

If every matching middleware calls `next()`, the current legacy `notFound(c)` handler produces the final response.

An error thrown by `catchNotFound()` enters the `catch()` / `onError()` flow.

### Path and base-path scoping

Without an explicit path, both APIs register at `*` within the current base path. With a path, they only run for matching requests:

```ts
const api = new Hono().basePath('/api')

api.catch('/items/*', errorMiddleware)
api.catchNotFound('/items/*', notFoundMiddleware)
```

Fallback matching is independent of the HTTP method of the original request.

Calling `catch()` or `catchNotFound()` does not change the current route path used by subsequent chained route methods.

## Sub-application ordering

Fallback routes are flattened into the parent Router together with normal routes when `route()` mounts a sub-application.

Each route records its application nesting depth. The depth is incremented whenever the route crosses a `route()` boundary.

Matching fallback middleware is composed in this order:

1. deeper sub-application routes first
2. registration order among routes at the same depth

For example:

```ts
app.catch(async (c) => c.text(`app: ${c.error?.message}`, 500))

sub.catch(async (_c, next) => {
  console.log('sub')
  await next()
})

app.route('/sub', sub)
```

For an error under `/sub`, the sub-application middleware runs first. If it calls `next()`, execution continues to the parent middleware.

For nested applications, the order is therefore:

```text
nested application -> sub-application -> parent application
```

This priority is based on application nesting, not path specificity. `basePath()` alone does not increase the depth.

Within the same application depth, matching definitions follow normal registration order:

```ts
app.catch('*', globalMiddleware)
app.catch('/items/*', itemsMiddleware)
```

For `/items/...`, `globalMiddleware` runs first. If it returns a response without calling `next()`, `itemsMiddleware` is not reached.

The same ordering rules apply to `catchNotFound()`.

## Flattening semantics

Fallback selection uses the original request path and the nesting depth of the matching fallback routes. It does not use the originating normal handler to establish an application ownership boundary.

For example, a parent route registered directly at `/api/example` may enter fallback middleware imported from an application mounted at `/api` because the request path matches that internal route.

Likewise, an error thrown by parent middleware while handling `/api/...` may enter the mounted API's error middleware.

This is consistent with the existing flattening model used by `route()` for paths and middleware.

Legacy `onError()` remains application-bound for compatibility. A sub-application with its own `onError()` continues to use that handler for errors thrown by its imported normal handlers.

## Error origin metadata

Internal dispatch does not overwrite the original route index.

Route parameters and origin-sensitive information such as `routePath(c)` therefore continue to describe the original route while fallback middleware runs.

If middleware throws after `await next()`, Hono restores the route index to the middleware that actually threw before dispatching the error middleware.

This separates three concerns:

- the request path determines which fallback routes match
- application depth determines sub-application priority
- the original route metadata describes where the fallback originated

## Internal routes and route metadata

Registrations made through `catch()` and `catchNotFound()` appear in `app.routes` with methods beginning with `@`.

The `@` prefix is reserved for internal routes. Internal methods are excluded from:

- `inspectRoutes()` / `showRoutes()`
- the `Allow` header generated by `methodNotAllowed()`

All routes created by Hono also carry depth metadata describing how many `route()` boundaries they have crossed.

Code that directly consumes `app.routes` may need to account for these additions.

If exposing internal routes through `app.routes` is undesirable, they can instead be kept in a completely separate internal collection. An earlier prototype showed that this was possible, but added roughly another 130 B to the minified bundle.

## Semantics preserved

- Existing `onError(error, c)` and `notFound(c)` signatures are unchanged.
- Repeated `onError()` and `notFound()` calls retain the existing last-assignment-wins behavior.
- Existing applications do not need to register `catch()` or `catchNotFound()`.
- Existing sub-application `onError()` behavior is preserved.
- `c.notFound()` is not a control-flow terminator. Its response must still be returned or awaited when it should become the route response.
- The default 404 and 500 responses are unchanged.
- Default `HTTPException#getResponse()` handling is unchanged.
- Internal dispatch reuses the original `Context`.
- Route parameters remain available while fallback middleware runs.
- Global `app.use()` middleware is not executed a second time during internal dispatch.
- An error thrown by a legacy error handler is still propagated.
- Successful normal routes do not pass through error or not-found middleware.

For example, this retains its existing behavior:

```ts
app.get('/', (c) => {
  c.notFound()
  return c.text('OK')
})
```

To use the not-found response, the handler must return it:

```ts
app.get('/', (c) => {
  return c.notFound()
})
```

## Router integration

Fallback middleware is registered using the configured Router's existing `add()` method and selected through `match()`.

This broadens the scope of router-decoration features such as the one proposed in #5201. A Router wrapper can wrap, instrument, or otherwise decorate `catch()` and `catchNotFound()` middleware alongside normal route handlers.

The legacy final `onError()` and `notFound()` handlers remain stored handlers rather than routes. A terminal `catch()` or `catchNotFound()` handler can provide the fully routable equivalent, while preserving the old APIs for compatibility.

## Performance

Internal routing is only entered when:

- normal routing does not produce a response
- a returned `c.notFound()` is dispatched
- a handler or middleware throws an error

It does not add another Router match to successful requests.

The existing successful-request execution structure is retained:

| Request path | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Single matched handler | one Router match + direct fast path | one Router match + direct fast path |
| Multiple matched handlers | one Router match + `compose()` | one Router match + `compose()` |
| Not found / error | direct stored fallback handler | additional internal Router match |

The single-handler fast path remains in place, and no global fallback middleware layer is added to every request.

For successful requests involving middleware, `compose()` now evaluates one additional boolean condition when updating the route index. A very small regression is therefore theoretically possible.

A local 15-round microbenchmark measured:

| Successful request | `main` | This PR | Difference |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Single handler | 483.86 ns | 483.99 ns | +0.03% |
| With middleware | 772.21 ns | 769.75 ns | -0.32% |

These differences are within the observed benchmark noise.

Matching fallback routes are sorted by application depth before composition. This work occurs only during error or not-found dispatch and only when fallback middleware matched.

The existing wrapper used to preserve a mounted sub-application's custom `onError()` remains for compatibility. The new routable fallback middleware itself is flattened without adding wrappers to successful normal routes.

## Bundle size

Measured from clean builds based on `cf785287b` using the existing bundle-size configuration. Compressed sizes were generated deterministically with gzip level 9 and Brotli quality 11.

| | `main` | This PR | Difference |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Minified | 19,000 B | 19,636 B | +636 B (+3.35%) |
| gzip -9 | 7,836 B | 8,102 B | +266 B (+3.39%) |
| Brotli q11 | 7,148 B | 7,395 B | +247 B (+3.46%) |

The internal methods are defined inside `hono-base.ts`; they are not added to the public Router API.

## Appendix: Design alternatives and trade-offs

Several API, fallback-selection, and storage models were explored. The current branch favors compatibility with the existing handlers and predictable sub-application ordering over the smaller but less compatible initial implementation.

The size estimates below come from earlier prototypes and should be treated as directional. If a larger bundle-size increase or different semantics are acceptable, some of these designs can be revisited.

### Adding middleware directly to `onError()` and `notFound()`

The initial implementation allowed middleware to be passed directly to the existing APIs:

```ts
app.notFound(languageDetector(), renderNotFound)
app.onError(languageDetector(), renderError)
```

This looked compact, but changed repeated registrations from last-assignment-wins to route composition. It also made the meaning of chaining and the current route path ambiguous for existing code.

The current design leaves both existing APIs unchanged and introduces `catch()` and `catchNotFound()` for routable middleware.

### Deferring fallback registration

Another model interprets fallback registration as being deferred until the end of the current application or until the corresponding `route()` call.

This naturally places a sub-application's fallback before its parent's fallback.

However, actual deferred registration must account for nested applications, repeated mounts, registration after mounting, and the point at which the route table becomes final.

The current implementation achieves the intended ordering without buffering registrations. It records route depth during `route()` and sorts only the matched fallback routes before composition.

### Selecting fallbacks from the originating application

An earlier implementation preserved the base path of the normal route that initiated fallback dispatch.

It selected:

1. a fallback registered at the exact originating base path
2. the root fallback when no exact definition existed

This prevented a parent route whose URL happened to be below a mounted application from entering the mounted application's fallback.

It also meant that:

- an implicit `/api/unknown` used the root fallback because it had no originating route
- a parent handler registered directly at `/api/example` used the parent fallback
- a handler imported through `app.route('/api', subApp)` used the sub-application fallback

This provides a stronger application boundary, but `app.route()` otherwise flattens paths and middleware into the parent routing space. Using handler provenance only for fallback selection therefore introduced a separate ownership model that did not apply to normal routing.

The implementation also required carrying the originating base path through dispatch, selecting an exact scope manually, and forwarding that scope through error handling. The earlier prototype added approximately another 200 B to the minified bundle compared with the flattened model at that time.

The current design keeps origin metadata for inspection but does not use it to select fallback middleware.

### Selecting the most specific path scope

Another prototype selected only the most specific matching internal path scope, independently of registration order.

This makes a scoped fallback reliably override a root fallback:

```ts
app.catchNotFound('*', renderAppNotFound)
app.catchNotFound('/api/*', renderApiNotFound)
```

Under that model, `/api/unknown` would always use `renderApiNotFound`, regardless of which definition was registered first.

However, Hono normally composes matching routes in registration order. Adding an independent path-specificity rule only for fallback routes would introduce a second ordering model.

A segment-aware implementation also required scanning and comparing matched scopes. The earlier prototype added approximately 126 B to the minified bundle compared with composing matching internal routes directly.

The current implementation distinguishes application nesting from path specificity. Deeper `route()` applications run first, while definitions at the same application depth retain registration order.

### Keeping internal routes outside `app.routes`

Internal routes could be stored in a completely separate collection while still being registered with the configured Router.

This would prevent raw `app.routes` consumers from seeing methods such as `@NOT_FOUND` and `@ERROR`.

However, it would require separate storage and mounting logic for internal routes. The earlier prototype increased the minified bundle by roughly another 130 B.

The selected implementation keeps a single route collection and filters reserved methods from user-facing helpers and the `Allow` header.

### Making `c.notFound()` a control-flow terminator

A terminal model was also considered, where calling `c.notFound()` would immediately stop the current handler even if its result was not returned:

```ts
app.get('/', (c) => {
  c.notFound()
  return c.text('unreachable')
})
```

Implementing this required a special control-flow signal to survive middleware composition and asynchronous handlers. It also changed how user `try` / `catch` blocks and upstream middleware observed the call.

The additional machinery was relatively large, and the behavior would differ substantially from the existing function-call semantics.

The current implementation therefore preserves the requirement to return or await `c.notFound()`.

### Reusing the normal request dispatch path

Internal fallback could have been implemented by re-entering the complete normal dispatch path with a reserved method or internal URL.

That would reduce the conceptual distinction between normal and fallback routing, but would either:

- create another `Request` or `Context`
- execute global middleware a second time
- add conditionals or wrappers to the successful-request path

These consequences conflict with the goal of preserving the original context and normal-request performance.

The selected implementation performs a separate Router match only after fallback dispatch has already been requested.

### Removing per-route wrappers for legacy sub-application errors

A sub-application with a custom `onError()` currently wraps its imported normal handlers so errors can be delegated to that stored handler.

Removing these wrappers would simplify the flattening model and allow every error handler to be represented only as a route. However, it would change the existing sub-application `onError()` behavior.

The current implementation retains the wrapper for the legacy API and adds routable `catch()` middleware alongside it. A future major version could reconsider the legacy handler after a migration path exists.

### The author should do the following, if applicable

- [x] Add tests
- [x] Run tests
- [x] `bun run format:fix && bun run lint:fix` to format the code
- [x] Add TSDoc/JSDoc where applicable

items.title: etag: PR #5205's chunked digest re-introduces #5199's hash(hash(chunk1)+chunk2) bug for bodies >= 256KB
items.body:
#5205 reintroduces the exact bug #5199 was written to fix, just anchored to fixed 256KB boundaries instead of network-arbitrary ones. For any response body of 256KB or more, the ETag middleware's SHA-1 digest no longer matches a real SHA-1 of the response body.

#5199's own description named the problem precisely: `result = generator(mergeBuffers(result, value))` computes `hash(hash(chunk1) + chunk2)` instead of `hash(chunk1 + chunk2)`, mathematically wrong, and depends on chunk boundaries. The fix was to buffer everything and hash once.

#5205's chunked accumulator does the same `result = await generator(mergeBuffers(result, chunk))` call, just triggered every `CHUNK_SIZE` (256 * 1024) bytes of the *cumulative* stream instead of on network-delivered chunk boundaries:

```ts
const digest = async (body) => {
  result = await generator(mergeBuffers(result, body))
}
```

This does make the digest deterministic for a given payload (chunking now depends only on total byte count, not network fragmentation, so #5199's original "same content, different ETag" symptom doesn't come back). But the resulting value stops being a real hash of the content the moment a response crosses 256KB, since `generator` here is a plain, stateless SHA-1 (`crypto.subtle.digest({name: 'SHA-1'}, body)`, no incremental/streaming hash API involved), and repeatedly re-hashing a digest concatenated with the next chunk does not reconstruct `SHA-1(full body)`.

Verified against Node's Web Crypto implementation rather than assuming the two would diverge:

```js
import { webcrypto as crypto } from 'node:crypto'

// 600KB body: 2 full 256KB chunks + a partial one, matching a realistic large response
const body = new Uint8Array(600 * 1024)
for (let i = 0; i < body.length; i++) body[i] = i % 256

const real = Buffer.from(await crypto.subtle.digest({name:'SHA-1'}, body)).toString('hex')
// chunkedDigest mirrors PR #5205's accumulate-then-digest loop exactly
const chunked = await chunkedDigest(body)

console.log(real)    // 239b1f5be294aa63293a407c9a050b1ab67655d6
console.log(chunked) // 1424154447f67661dc50a1fc6a2c589151e18013
console.log(real === chunked) // false
```

Anything relying on the ETag actually being the response's SHA-1 (external cache validation against a separately-computed hash, `Digest`/`Content-Digest` header comparisons, CDN-side dedup by content hash) breaks silently for responses at or above 256KB. It's also specifically the size range the original memory-pressure concern was about, so the two fixes are pulling in opposite directions: correct-but-unbounded-memory (#5199) vs bounded-memory-but-mathematically-wrong-hash (#5205) for large bodies.

If bounded memory is the goal, a real incremental hash needs an actual incremental hash primitive that supports it (Node's `crypto.createHash('sha1').update(chunk)` streaming API, for example, which properly maintains SHA-1's internal state across `update()` calls instead of re-hashing an already-hashed digest each time), not repeated whole-buffer re-digests of the previous digest.

items.title: fix(etag): resolve incorrect incremental hashing for chunked responses
items.body:
Resolves #4401. Hono's `etag` middleware previously generated ETags for streams by hashing chunks incrementally using `result = generator(mergeBuffers(result, value))`. This computes `hash(hash(chunk1) + chunk2)` instead of `hash(chunk1 + chunk2)`.
Consequently, the generated ETag was mathematically incorrect and depended on how the response stream chunks were split across the network.

This PR fixes the digest generation logic in `generateDigest` to accumulate all stream chunks in memory first and perform a single SHA-1 hash on the full payload, ensuring mathematical correctness and consistency across chunk sizes. Additionally, the middleware now skips ETag generation for `text/event-stream` (SSE) responses to prevent infinite reader blocking and hangs.

 ###  Design Decisions & Rationale

* **Buffer-and-Hash for Correctness:** Native Web Crypto (`crypto.subtle.digest`) does not support streaming/incremental hashing. To calculate the correct SHA-1 hash of the response body, we must collect the stream chunks in memory and merge them. This ensures that identical response payloads always yield the same ETag, regardless of network chunk fragmentation or compression differences.

* **Targeted SSE Bypass:** Server-Sent Events (SSE) are infinite streams. Trying to read them to the end blocks the reader indefinitely. We added a zero-overhead check for the `Content-Type: text/event-stream` header to bypass the ETag pipeline safely.

* **Memory Trade-off:** While buffering chunks consumes memory proportional to the response body, the ETag middleware already clones and reads the entire body stream to hash it. Consolidating the chunks in memory is a minor overhead that is necessary to achieve cache specification compliance.
